The assistance includes food, essential medicines and other immediate requirements wherever needed and feasible, it said. The mission also said it remained in regular contact with Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Hajj and Umrah and Ministry of Foreign Affairs to address difficulties caused by the flight disruptions, particularly issues concerning visa validity and delayed departures. Meanwhile, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is preparing to resume domestic and international flight operations on Sunday, the Gulf News web portal reported. It also quoted the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis as saying on Sunday that air defences had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh.

The coordinated missile salvo represents ongoing tension between Saudi military forces and Yemen's Houthi movement. Saudi forces maintain operational readiness using advanced air defence equipment, including MIM-104 Patriot systems, to counter incoming cross-border missile and drone projectiles.

news.headline: Delhi gets pollution source data, but a big chunk stays unexplained
news.story_lead: Delhi gets pollution source data, but a big chunk stays unexplained The accompanying forecast model uses an emissions estimate based on older surveys, limiting confidence until it is updated. The Capital has its first breakdown of air pollution by source in nearly three years. But the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology ’s (IITM) new measurements cannot yet say where a large share of the pollution they measure comes from, and its air pollution prediction model still runs on a 2021 emissions estimate that its own website says needs updating, with a replacement expected only by June next year.
news.full_article_text: Delhi gets pollution source data, but a big chunk stays unexplained The accompanying forecast model uses an emissions estimate based on older surveys, limiting confidence until it is updated. The Capital has its first breakdown of air pollution by source in nearly three years. But the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology ’s (IITM) new measurements cannot yet say where a large share of the pollution they measure comes from, and its air pollution prediction model still runs on a 2021 emissions estimate that its own website says needs updating, with a replacement expected only by June next year. Particles labelled “secondary sources” --- these form in the air due to a phenomenon that involves an interaction between gases — made up 29.3% to 42.2% of the new lab’s daily estimate of PM2.5 from October 20 to 24. The five days IITM’s page showed on Saturday evening put these sources ahead of vehicles at 19.4% to 27.6%, HT’s analysis of the numbers showed. Officials said they have no system yet to break these secondary aerosols down by their origin. A second problem was that the lab’s total PM2.5 reading was itself far below what Delhi ’s monitors recorded. For instance, it was 55.3 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) on October 22. That number was 47% of a middle reading of 117.1 µg/m³ among 37 stations that day, a comparison with Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) air quality data from that day showed. When this was pointed out by HT, officials said the site was still new and facing teething issues. “The PM 2.5 data will reflect accurately, shortly,” an official said. Sachin Ghude, the IITM scientist overseeing the lab, said a large chunk of particulate matter originated as secondary pollutants: “Unlike primary, which are emitted directly into the air, secondary aerosols form when gases undergo chemical reactions in the atmosphere and get converted into particles.” Also Read | Delhi AQI 'moderate' at 191; environment minister says govt in 'war mode for clean air' Secondary organic aerosols form from volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and secondary inorganic ones, such as sulphates and nitrates, from gases including sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia. “We are working on that now, to try and find how these are forming. While we know this is a complex reaction of gases and VOCs, the original source is not known,” Ghude told HT. The lab’s next phase, he said, will first split the vehicle share between diesel, compressed natural gas (CNG) and petrol vehicles, which he expects “in a fortnight or so”. The big gap in understanding the source could well hamper the effort’s usefulness. “This facility will help us understand the composition of pollution as well as the contribution of different sources,” said Union minister of state for science and technology Jitendra Singh, while inaugurating the lab, called the Advanced Atmospheric Chemistry and Aerosol Toxicity Analysis Laboratory (Aatal) at New Rajendra Nagar, on Saturday. He added that this was important for “ensuring that action is based on scientific evidence”. The lab’s 25 instruments, for atmospheric chemistry, source apportionment (working out how much pollution comes from each source) and aerosol toxicity, cost about ₹ 80 crore. The ministry of earth sciences said the lab will complement IITM’s Air Quality Early Warning System and its Decision Support System (DSS), the prediction model whose source split the new web page shows by default; the DSS forecast for Saturday put Delhi’s transport at 17.7%. Also Read | New GRAP actions failed to curb Delhi-NCR pollution in 10 of 12 episodes, reveals study The model’s 2021 emissions inventory, its estimate of what each source releases, was “compiled using surveys done in 2016”, according to a 2024 paper by IITM scientists, and a replacement with a 2026 baseline is due only by June 2027. IITM’s DSS page acknowledges “the latest emission fields are required” for more accurate estimates, and a second 2024 paper, summarised on its methodology page, says the model does not simulate nitrate or secondary organic aerosols, which alone made up 15.5% to 21.2% of the lab’s daily estimate. A senior government official said the lab’s data would add to the DSS, but the overall assessment would not become fully accurate until the inventory is updated, which officials expect to happen next year. What the estimate shows Vehicles and the two secondary categories were the lab’s three largest of 15 every day. Its seven burning categories together made up 20.5% to 35.6% in HT’s sum, crop-residue burning alone 2.5% to 4.7%, and road, soil and construction dust 3.8% to 20.6%. On October 22, after IITM’s revision, burning was the largest group in HT’s sums, at 35.0% against 33.8% for the two secondary categories, the only day it was. IITM’s page names vehicles the “dominant contribution” each day by skipping both secondary categories. On October 23, secondary organic aerosols alone edged vehicles, 19.5% to 19.4%. The new page calls the split “real-time” but gives one figure a day per category, with no hourly data or method. IITM’s older Analysis page shows the lab’s daily figures in a chart marked “Experimental Mode - Preliminary results” and labelled a source contribution of “NR-PM2.5”, a term the site does not explain, where the new page says “Total PM2.5 (sum of the listed sources)”. At 6.18pm on Saturday the new page also showed Friday and a part-day Saturday reading, with vehicles at 25%; by 6.30pm both had gone. They were back by 9.28pm, revised along with Thursday, with Saturday’s total raised from 25.2 µg/m³ to 29.9 µg/m³ and its vehicle share from 25% to 27.6%; the older chart, updated at 8.49pm, now carries the revised figures, and the tab now shows October 20 to 24. The changes suggested tweaks were still being made. Also Read | Delhi minister orders crackdown on pollution hotspots as air remains ‘poor’ for 3rd day IITM’s note on the lab says the facility will quantify contributions from sources “including transport, industry, biomass burning, and regional pollution transport”. None of its 15 categories covers pollution from outside Delhi, and IITM has not said how it tells dung cake, wood, crop residue and other fuels apart. Sunil Dahiya, founder and lead analyst at the think-tank Envirocatalysts, said the true value of real-time source apportionment, forecasting and meteorological tools “depends entirely on data accuracy, lower model uncertainties, and actual real time availability”. Delhi’s previous source studies, by IIT Kanpur in 2016 and The Energy and Resources Institute in 2018, are dated. news.headline: Amid Jamia row, ABVP claims ‘Free Umar Khalid’, ‘Long Live Naxalbari’ slogans written on JNU walls, seeks action
news.story_lead: Amid Jamia row, ABVP claims ‘Free Umar Khalid’, ‘Long Live Naxalbari’ slogans written on JNU walls, seeks action ABVP's claims over the alleged slogans on the JNU walls comes two days after similar slogans were allegedly spotted at Jamia Millia Islamia University. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) has alleged that “provocative slogans” such as “Free Umar Khalid” and “Long Live Naxalbari” were written on the walls of Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), urging the administration to take cognisance of the incidents and appropriate action against those responsible. This comes two days after similar slogans were allegedly spotted at Jamia Millia Islamia University in the capital.
news.full_article_text: Amid Jamia row, ABVP claims ‘Free Umar Khalid’, ‘Long Live Naxalbari’ slogans written on JNU walls, seeks action ABVP's claims over the alleged slogans on the JNU walls comes two days after similar slogans were allegedly spotted at Jamia Millia Islamia University. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) has alleged that “provocative slogans” such as “Free Umar Khalid” and “Long Live Naxalbari” were written on the walls of Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), urging the administration to take cognisance of the incidents and appropriate action against those responsible. This comes two days after similar slogans were allegedly spotted at Jamia Millia Islamia University in the capital. In a post on X, Vishva Hindu Parishad (VHP) national spokesperson Vinod Bansal shared photographs purportedly showing graffiti, including “Free Kashmir”, “Free Palestine”, “Free Sharjeel Imam” and “RSS Go Back”, on the campus walls. At JNU, the ABVP also claimed that objectionable content had been written on a portrait of VD Savarkar. Also Read | Congress, Samajwadi Party MPs detained on way to join Jamia Millia students’ protest in Delhi “Freedom of expression must go hand in hand with responsibility and respect for public property and differing viewpoints. Universities should be spaces for constructive debate, not provocation and confrontation. ABVP JNU demands that the university administration take cognisance of these incidents, identify those responsible, and take appropriate action to safeguard the dignity and academic atmosphere of the campus,” ABVP JNU said in a post on X on Saturday. The JNU administration has reportedly taken cognisance of the matter and is looking into it, saying it would not allow vested interests to disturb peace on the campus. Why are Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in jail? Umar Khalid, a former JNU research scholar, has been in jail since September 2020 in connection with the larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 Delhi riots. He has been charged under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA). The case relates to violence that left 53 people dead in the national capital. Sharjeel Imam, another former JNU scholar, was arrested in 2020 over speeches delivered during protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA). A case was filed against him under sedition and other charges following a speech at Aligarh Muslim University in which he called for blocking roads connecting the Northeast with the rest of India. Protests in Jamia Millia Islamia The controversy over the slogans comes amid intensifying protests at Jamia Millia Islamia over the restoration of the students' union. Students have also demanded the revocation of disciplinary action against students and the removal of the university's chief proctor over what they have described as a crackdown on protesters. Tensions flared between teaching staff and students on Saturday amid allegations of a forceful confrontation between the two sides. As a result, the university shifted classes to online mode . Speaking to reporters, Jamia Registrar Rizvi said he had personally met students staging a hunger strike and discussed their demand for students' union elections. “Regarding their demand for holding a union election, I informed them that we have already formed a draft committee tasked with drafting a constitution. They then asked for a deadline. I told them that the sooner they complete the draft constitution, the sooner we will conduct the elections—a proposal they agreed to,” the registrar said, according to news agency ANI. On Saturday, Congress leader Imran Masood visited the Jamia campus and dismissed reports of “Free Kashmir” slogans being raised there as fake news. However, he acknowledged that some posters carrying the same slogan had been put up on the campus and demanded strict action against those responsible. Rizvi also condemned the “Free Kashmir” graffiti reportedly found on the campus. “As for the graffiti written yesterday—the 'Free Kashmir' slogan—we condemn it in the strongest possible terms; we will not support it under any circumstances,” he said. Protesting students alleged that the controversial posters were being put up to create a different narrative amid the ongoing demonstrations. news.full_article_text: Meerut ‘blue drum’ murder convicts Muskan, Sahil challenge death sentence in high court They argue the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the trial court relied on speculation. Muskan Rastogi and Sahil Shukla, the two convicts sentenced to death in the Saurabh Rajput murder case in Meerut , have approached the Allahabad high court challenging their conviction and the death sentence awarded to them by the trial court. The duo have filed criminal appeals seeking the quashing of the Meerut district and sessions court’s orders convicting them on September 30 and sentencing them to death on October 14, 2026. A division bench of the high court is likely to hear the matter next week. The case, widely known as the ‘blue drum’ murder case, relates to the killing of Saurabh Rajput in the Brahmpuri police station area of Meerut. The case triggered widespread outrage after his body was found concealed in a blue plastic drum filled with cement and concrete. They were also convicted of offences related to causing the disappearance of evidence. In their appeals, the convicts have described the trial court’s verdict as illegal and arbitrary, seeking the setting aside of their conviction and sentence and their acquittal of all charges under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The appellants have contended that the prosecution failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt. They argued that the case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence, but the trial court reached its conclusions on the basis of speculation and conjecture, allegedly overlooking established legal principles. - Allahabad High Court

Adequate police personnel have been deployed along VVIP routes, at the event venue and in sensitive areas. Drones have also been deployed and CCTV cameras have been installed in these areas,” he said. “Clear orders have been given that there should be no laxity during the air show and the Prime Minister’s visit. While ensuring VVIP security, all officers and personnel must prioritise public convenience, safe movement and crowd management,” he added. The slaughter and sale of meat have also been prohibited within a 20-30-kilometre radius of the event venue from October 19 to 26. news.story_lead: Vanessa Trump and her 19-year-old daughter Kai - Published 24 October 2026, 15:45 BST Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year. Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free". Following the Instagram post on Friday, Vanessa and Kai Trump released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention.
news.full_article_text: Vanessa Trump and her 19-year-old daughter Kai - Published 24 October 2026, 15:45 BST Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year. Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free". Following the Instagram post on Friday, Vanessa and Kai Trump released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention. Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods. "October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram. "I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued. Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben. Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour. "It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results. "You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you." Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team. She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said. According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group. Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk. Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.
